claims.claim: Sort the cells in your body by size, from red blood cells up, and something odd turns up: each size class weighs roughly the same.
claims.where: spoken (hook)
claims.source_checked: Hatton et al. 2023, PNAS 120(39) e2303077120, doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120, full text PMC10523466 (Europe PMC fullTextXML) and Fig. 4 image (cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov blob pnas.2303077120fig04.jpg)
claims.note: Abstract: 'all cells within a given logarithmic size class contribute an equal fraction to the body's total cellular biomass'; Results: 'a roughly similar fraction of total body mass is present in each logarithmic cell-size class'; Significance calls the inverse relation 'surprising'. The hook is the paper's own headline at the paper's own hedge ('roughly'), so a viewer leaving at second two keeps a true claim. The dip is the paper's stated exception and is drawn on the hook card's bars. 'Your body' generalises the reference male/female/child models, which the paper calls 'broadly similar'. Size = cell mass, the paper's measure; binning starts at red blood cells (Methods).

claims.claim: On-screen hook card: 'ROUGHLY THE SAME' over schematic weight bars on a log cell-mass ruler (10^-11 to 10^-2 g, labelled 'CELL MASS IN GRAMS · LOG SCALE', bars labelled 'WEIGHT IN EACH CLASS · LOG SCALE · SCHEMATIC').
claims.where: on-screen: ROUGHLY THE SAME (cards 1 and 20), Ruler weights
claims.note: Bars occupy 26 octave classes from 4e-11 g (Methods: 'beginning at the lower bound of erythrocytes, and giving 26 size classes'); last edge 4e-11*2^26 = 2.7e-3 g fits Fig. 3's range. Bars are level with a dip between ~1.9e-6 and ~6e-5 g and raised bins near 1e-6 g (fat) and 1e-4 to 2e-4 g (muscle), matching Fig. 4's peaks and gap in shape. Heights are not data and the card says 'SCHEMATIC' (A6).

claims.claim: A twenty twenty-three study combined over fifteen hundred published sources to estimate the body's cells, type by type, and sorted them by size.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen: 1,500+ SOURCES
claims.source_checked: PMC10523466 (abstract, Approach, Methods; published online 18 Sep 2023)
claims.note: Abstract: 'data drawn from >1,500 published sources'; Methods: 'more than 1,500 published sources for 400 known cell types across 60 tissue systems'; 'we estimate'. Size histogram built over cell types (Fig. 3). PNAS 2023.

claims.claim: The smallest cells it sorted are red blood cells.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen: RED BLOOD CELLS, mark 'FROM 4 × 10⁻¹¹ g' at 4e-11 g
claims.note: 'only considers the distribution beginning at red blood cells (4 × 10−11 g)'; Methods: 'We ignored binning cells smaller than erythrocytes (blood platelets and the smallest haploid gamete cells)'. 'It sorted' keeps the claim to the binning, so platelets being smaller does not contradict it. 4e-11 g is the paper's value and 'FROM' correctly marks it as the start of the range.

claims.claim: The biggest are muscle fibres, more than a million times heavier.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen: >1,000,000× HEAVIER, mark 'MUSCLE FIBRES ~10⁻⁴ g'
claims.note: 'from a tiny red blood cell to a myocyte, more than a million-fold larger'; sizes span 'seven orders of magnitude from red blood cells to the largest muscle fibers'; size is cell mass, so 'heavier' is right. Mark ~1e-4 g = 'myocytes (near 10−4 g)' biomass peak; 1e-4/4e-11 = 2.5 million, consistent with '>1,000,000×'.

claims.claim: Now put those cells into size classes, where each class holds cells twice as heavy as the one before.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen: ×2 CELL SIZE, 27 bin edges drawn from 4e-11 g
claims.note: 'bins increase by a multiplicative factor of 2 from small to large (octave size classes), beginning at the lower bound of erythrocytes, and giving 26 size classes'. Code draws exactly 26 classes from 4e-11 g.

claims.claim: Each time the size doubles, there are, on average, about half as many cells.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen: HALF AS MANY
claims.source_checked: PMC10523466 Fig. 3 caption and image, Methods
claims.note: Count per class follows 'a power law with a slope near −0.97 with a 95% CI of −1.09 to −0.87'. 2^-0.97 = 0.51 (CI 0.47 to 0.55) per doubling, so 'about half'. 'On average' fits a fitted trend.

claims.claim: Count staircase: falling bars per class, labelled 'NUMBER OF CELLS · LOG SCALE · SCHEMATIC', with a drop in the classes between fat and muscle.
claims.where: on-screen: Ruler counts (cards 6 and 7)
claims.note: Linear fall in log count across the 26 classes matches the ~-1 slope. Fig. 3's binned counts fall well below the fit around 5e-6 to 3e-5 g (about 1 to 1.5 decades), which the drawn dip (classes with mid 1.9e-6 to 5.9e-5 g) shows in schematic form. Labelled schematic.

claims.claim: So the small cells win on numbers, the big cells win on size, and the two cancel out.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen: THEY CANCEL OUT
claims.note: 'an increase in size by a given factor is offset by a decrease in cell count by a similar factor... Such an inverse relation implies that a roughly similar fraction of total body mass is present in each logarithmic cell-size class'. 'Cancel out' = 'offset'.

claims.claim: Every class ends up holding roughly the same weight.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen: ABOUT THE SAME
claims.note: As claim 1: 'roughly similar fraction... in each logarithmic cell-size class'; Conclusion: 'cell biomass is roughly independent of cell-size class'. The next sentence gives the paper's one stated exception.

claims.claim: With one exception: a dip, between the fat cells and the muscle fibres.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen: ONE DIP, marks 'FAT CELLS ~10⁻⁶ g' and 'MUSCLE FIBRES ~10⁻⁴ g'
claims.note: 'prominent biomass peaks comprising adipocytes (near 10−6 g) and myocytes (near 10−4 g), separated by a gap of relatively low biomass'; 'With the exception of this gap, all variation in cellular biomass lies within two orders of magnitude'. The paper also notes breaks near platelets and sperm (~1e-11 g), but those are outside the binned range, so 'one exception' holds within the sorted classes. Mark values are the paper's.

claims.claim: In a typical woman the dip is smaller, and in a typical ten-year-old it is fainter still.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen: TYPICAL WOMAN; THE DIP BETWEEN FAT AND MUSCLE; rows 'TYPICAL MAN: MOST PROMINENT', 'TYPICAL WOMAN: SMALLER', 'TYPICAL 10-YEAR-OLD: FAINTER STILL'
claims.note: 'This gap is also evident but less prominent in the reference female, and is even less evident in the 10-y-old reference child'. 'Most prominent' for the man follows from the ordering of the three. 'Typical' = the paper's reference models (60 kg female, 32 kg 10-y child); the rows are text only, with no drawn values.

claims.claim: Take a typical man.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen: A TYPICAL MAN, sub '70 KG (154 LB)'
claims.note: Reference male: '70 kg, 176 cm in height and 20 to 50 y of age'. 70 kg = 154.3 lb.

claims.claim: His muscle fibres are fewer than one in fifty thousand of his cells with a nucleus.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen: < 1 IN 50,000; dot grid '50,000 CELLS WITH A NUCLEUS · AT MOST 1 MUSCLE FIBRE'
claims.note: Skeletal myocytes 'make up <0.002% of the nucleated cell count' (reference male). 0.002% = 1/50,000, an upper bound, so 'fewer than' and 'at most 1' are right. The grid is 250 x 200 = 50,000 dots with one highlighted (code). 'Muscle fibres' here means skeletal muscle fibres, the usual sense and the paper's 'skeletal myocytes'.

claims.claim: Yet they make up about half the weight of all his cells.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen: ABOUT HALF; MUSCLE FIBRES ≈ HALF (bar 22.5 of 45 kg)
claims.note: 'Cell biomass is dominated by skeletal myocytes, comprising about half of all 45 kg of cell biomass'; 'the remaining 23.5 kg' implies ~21.5 kg (48%). A half-length bar is right for 'about half'.

claims.claim: And all his cells together weigh about forty-five kilograms.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen: 45 KG, sub '99 LB'; ALL HIS CELLS · 45 KG
claims.note: 'all 45 kg of cell biomass in the body' (reference male). 45 kg = 99.2 lb.

claims.claim: The other twenty-five of his seventy are not cells at all. They are the water, protein and minerals between them.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen: NOT CELLS, sub '25 KG (55 LB)'; NOT CELLS · 25 KG; 70 KG MAN; BETWEEN THE CELLS; WATER · PROTEIN · MINERALS; bar 45 + 25 of 70 kg
claims.note: Cell biomass 'excludes noncellular components of biomass in each tissue, made up of extracellular water, protein, and minerals (~25 kg)'. 45 + 25 = 70 kg reference male. 'Between them' = extracellular. 25 kg = 55.1 lb. Bar proportions 45:25 of 70 match.

claims.claim: Sort the life in the ocean by size, as it was before industrial fishing, and most size classes held about the same weight too.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen: THE OCEAN TOO
claims.source_checked: Hatton, Heneghan, Bar-On & Galbraith 2021, Sci. Adv. 7(46) eabh3732, doi:10.1126/sciadv.abh3732, full text PMC8580314 (Europe PMC fullTextXML) and Fig. 2 image
claims.note: Abstract: 'biomass within most order of magnitude size classes is indeed remarkably constant, near 1 gigatonne... but bacteria and large marine mammals are markedly above and below this value'. Evaluated 'before industrial-scale human capture of fish and marine mammals (pre-1850)'; today 'the upper one-third of the biomass spectrum has been severely truncated', so the past tense and 'most' are right. The PNAS paper cites it as the same pattern ('bodies in the ocean from bacteria to whales'). The script does not claim the same class width.

claims.claim: Ocean card: bars on a log axis 'SIZE OF SEA LIFE, BACTERIA TO WHALES · LOG SCALE', titled 'BEFORE INDUSTRIAL FISHING · SCHEMATIC', with the first three classes raised and the last two lowered.
claims.where: on-screen: BEFORE INDUSTRIAL FISHING · SCHEMATIC, Ruler ocean
claims.note: Fig. 2A (upper 200 m): first classes ~2.5, 2.5, 1.9 Gt (bacteria/autotrophs), most others ~1 Gt, last two mammal classes ~0.1 Gt; caption: 'approximately 1 Gt... with exceptions at either extreme'. The drawing shows that shape and says 'SCHEMATIC'. It draws 26 bars, not the paper's ~23 order-of-magnitude classes, and has no tick values, so no class count or width is claimed.

claims.claim: And in your body, nobody knows why. No accepted process explains it yet.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen: NOBODY KNOWS WHY; NOT YET EXPLAINED
claims.source_checked: PMC10523466 Discussion (Origins) and Conclusion; firecrawl web search for later work (no established mechanism found)
claims.note: 'To our knowledge, there is no universally recognized process that accounts for these patterns'; Conclusion: 'the developmental mechanisms underlying this pattern remain unresolved'. The paper offers candidates (random growth, mismatched growth and division rates) but does not claim they are established, so 'no accepted process... yet' is exact and 'nobody knows why' is a fair plain rendering. The source dates from 2023. A search found no later accepted explanation, but that search was not exhaustive.

claims.claim: Trillions of tiny cells, far fewer giant ones, and roughly the same weight at almost every size.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen: ROUGHLY THE SAME (final card, marks for red blood cells, fat cells, muscle fibres)
claims.note: ≈36 trillion cells in the reference male, ≈29 trillion of them nonnucleated blood cells (red cells and platelets), so there are trillions of the smallest cells. Large cells are far fewer (myocytes <0.002% of nucleated cells). 'Almost every size' accounts for the dip, and 'roughly' matches the paper's wording.

claims.claim: Where else do you think this pattern shows up?
claims.where: spoken; on-screen: WHERE ELSE?
claims.note: A question, not a claim. Its presupposition that the pattern appears elsewhere is supported: 'This size distribution appears to be common in nature... cities, asteroids and bodies in the ocean from bacteria to whales'.
